script.opening: "Honestly I don’t know why my partner made such a fuss about me booking this. I’m FINE — I’m just tired, all new mums are knackered, aren’t they? The baby’s lovely, everything’s lovely. I think I just need to get more sleep and pull myself together. Can you just tell him I’m okay so he stops hovering? I really don’t want to be one of those mums who can’t cope."

facts.text: If explored gently: persistent low mood for >3–4 weeks (beyond "baby blues"), tearfulness, anhedonia, can’t sleep even when the baby does (not just sleep deprivation), poor appetite, profound guilt ("terrible mother"), poor concentration, and a sense of detachment / not bonding with the baby. This is postnatal depression, not normal tiredness.

CRITICAL, on sensitive direct questioning: thoughts that the baby/family "would be better off without me", and frightening intrusive thoughts (e.g. of harm coming to the baby) that horrify her and which she’s told no one about. Must assess: thoughts of self-harm/suicide (plan/intent/means), thoughts of harming the baby, and ability to care for the baby. Red flags for severe illness / puerperal psychosis must be screened (though here the picture is severe depression). Because she has passive thoughts of being better off gone, NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) review within 1 week of starting any antidepressant applies; NICE NG225 (2022): no risk-scoring tools or low/medium/high ratings — a safety plan built with her instead.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the minimising is driven by TERROR that admitting she’s struggling means social services will "take the baby away" and that she’ll be judged an unfit mother. This fear is why she hides the intrusive thoughts and pushes for "tell him I’m fine". Naming and dismantling this fear (honest, reassuring information about how perinatal mental health support actually works) is the hinge of the consultation.

If reached: a traumatic forceps delivery she hasn’t processed, no family nearby, a sense of failure against an idealised "perfect mum", shame about not feeling the bond everyone expects. Her partner’s concern is the reliable signal.

Officially: to be told she’s fine so her partner stops worrying. What she needs: recognition of postnatal depression, a sensitive and explicit risk assessment (self and baby), the "they’ll take my baby" fear dismantled, and a supportive treatment plan (perinatal pathway, talking therapy, breastfeeding-compatible options).

ice.ideas: It’s just normal new-mum tiredness; she should pull herself together and sleep more.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror that admitting she’s struggling means social services will take the baby and she’ll be judged an unfit mother; this is why she hides the intrusive thoughts and minimises; trauma from the delivery, isolation, and shame about not bonding.
ice.expectations: To be reassured she’s fine. What she actually needs: recognition of postnatal depression, an explicit risk assessment (self + baby), the "they’ll take my baby" fear addressed honestly, and a supportive perinatal treatment plan.

cues: "I’m just tired, tell him I’m fine" — minimising; the partner’s concern is the reliable signal and fear is underneath.
Flat affect, tearful, "terrible mother", not bonding — postnatal depression, not baby blues (which resolves by ~2 weeks).
A flicker of shame/fear if asked about frightening thoughts — the hidden intrusive thoughts and the "they’ll take my baby" terror.

checkpoints.text: Recognises POSTNATAL DEPRESSION (pervasive low mood >2 weeks beyond the baby-blues window, anhedonia, guilt, sleep/appetite change, detachment from the baby) and does NOT accept "just normal tiredness" or advise her to "pull herself together"

Conducts an EXPLICIT, sensitive RISK ASSESSMENT: thoughts of self-harm/suicide (plan, intent, means), thoughts of harming the baby or intrusive thoughts, and her ability to care for the baby — asking directly and non-judgementally rather than avoiding it

Screens for and recognises red flags of SEVERE perinatal illness / puerperal psychosis (rapid onset, perplexity, mania, delusions/hallucinations, marked agitation, thoughts of harming the baby) — which would be a perinatal psychiatric EMERGENCY needing urgent specialist assessment

DISMANTLES the "they’ll take my baby" fear with honest information: perinatal mental health support is about helping her get well and stay WITH her baby, struggling is common and treatable, and seeking help is the protective, good-mother act — not a trigger for removal

Makes a supportive, appropriate plan (NICE CG192): perinatal/NHS Talking Therapies referral, psychological therapy first-line for mild–moderate, a high-intensity psychological intervention (e.g. CBT) for moderate–severe with an antidepressant considered if she prefers medication or therapy has not helped — choosing one with the BNF breastfeeding advice checked (sertraline is often chosen; dose per BNF), with discussion, health-visitor involvement, partner/social support, and follow-up matched to severity/risk

Hears the minimisation as fear, treats the partner’s concern as the reliable signal, and creates enough safety for her to disclose the intrusive thoughts rather than colluding with "tell him I’m fine"
Responds to the shame, the bonding fear and the birth trauma with warmth and normalisation, so she feels supported rather than judged

Safety-nets and follows up robustly: crisis routes if thoughts of harm to self/baby escalate (urgent perinatal/crisis team, 999), close follow-up, health visitor and partner engaged, and clear documentation of the risk assessment — balancing support with safety

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came, even if it was your partner’s nudge — partners usually notice these things because they love us and see us up close. I’m not going to just tell him you’re fine, because I’d rather actually check how YOU are, properly, with no rush. Is that okay?"

"What you’re describing — crying a lot, not sleeping even when the baby does, feeling detached, that horrible ‘terrible mother’ voice — that’s more than tiredness, and it’s not you failing. It sounds like postnatal depression, which is incredibly common and very treatable. The baby blues lift by about two weeks; this has gone on longer and deeper, and that’s worth treating, not toughing out."

"I ask every new mum these, because they matter and you’re not alone in them. When you feel this low — do you ever have thoughts that your family would be better off without you? … And sometimes mums get frightening thoughts pop into their heads, even about the baby coming to harm — thoughts that horrify them. Have you had anything like that? … Thank you for trusting me. Having those thoughts does NOT make you dangerous or a bad mother — it’s a symptom we can treat."

"Can I name something? I think part of why this has stayed hidden is a fear that if you admit you’re struggling, someone will take your baby away. Let me be really clear: that is not how this works. Everything we do is about helping you get well and keeping you and your baby together. Asking for help is the protective, good-mother thing to do — it’s the opposite of unfit."

"So here’s what I’d suggest, and we do it together: some proper support from the perinatal mental health and talking-therapy services, your health visitor more involved, and if you’d find it helpful, a medication that can be used while breastfeeding — sertraline is the one we often choose, after checking the breastfeeding advice for it — to lift the worst of it. None of this takes anything away from you; it gives you back to yourself and to your baby."

"If those darker thoughts ever get stronger, or you ever feel you might act on a thought about yourself or the baby, that’s when you contact us or the crisis team urgently, or 999 — I’ll give you exactly who to call. I want to speak to you again within a week, and your partner’s welcome too. You came in to be told you’re fine. What you’re actually getting is people who are going to help you feel like yourself again — you don’t have to carry this alone."

f.learning: Pervasive low mood beyond the two-week baby-blues window — anhedonia, guilt ("terrible mother"), sleep/appetite change, and detachment from the baby — is postnatal depression, not normal tiredness, and must not be met with "pull yourself together". The non-negotiable task is an EXPLICIT, sensitive risk assessment covering self-harm/suicide (plan, intent, means), thoughts of harming the baby or frightening intrusive thoughts, and ability to care for the baby — plus screening for red flags of puerperal psychosis (rapid onset, perplexity, mania, psychosis, thoughts of harming the baby), a perinatal psychiatric emergency. The examinable hidden agenda is the terror that disclosure means social services "taking the baby" — which drives the minimisation and the concealment of intrusive thoughts; dismantling it honestly (help is about keeping mother and baby together; seeking help is the protective act) is the hinge. Treat the partner’s concern as the reliable signal, respond to shame/bonding-fear/birth-trauma with warmth, and make a supportive plan (NICE CG192: perinatal pathway, psychological therapy, an antidepressant such as sertraline where indicated after checking the BNF breastfeeding advice, health visitor, partner) with robust risk-based safety-netting and review within 1 week (NICE NG222).

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health · NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022)
knowledge.summary: Low mood, loss of interest, guilt and detachment from the baby 8 weeks after birth is postnatal depression, not tiredness. Ask directly about thoughts of self-harm and of harm to the baby, screen for psychosis, and deal with the fear of the baby being taken away.

points.t: Baby blues are common in the first days after birth and settle within about 2 weeks. Symptoms lasting longer, with anhedonia, guilt, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and poor bonding, indicate a depressive episode.

NICE CG192: at contact in the postnatal period, ask the two depression identification questions (feeling down, depressed or hopeless; little interest or pleasure) and consider the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment. Tools support clinical judgement; they do not replace it.

Ask about thoughts of self-harm or suicide (plan, intent, means), thoughts of harm to the baby, intrusive thoughts, and her ability to care for the baby. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or low, medium or high ratings to predict suicide; build a safety plan around her needs.

Sudden onset of confusion, perplexity, mania, delusions or hallucinations is an emergency. NICE CG192: refer to secondary mental health services, preferably the specialist perinatal team, for assessment within 4 hours.

NICE CG192: for moderate or severe depression in the postnatal period, offer a high-intensity psychological intervention such as CBT; consider an antidepressant if she prefers medication, declines therapy or symptoms have not responded. Discuss breastfeeding: check the BNF breastfeeding advice for the chosen drug (sertraline is often chosen). Dose per BNF.

Fear that social services will take the baby is a common reason mothers hide symptoms. Most mothers with postnatal depression receive support to recover while caring for their baby; a safeguarding referral is made only where there is a risk to the child.

dg.d: Open question about life since the birth; doesn’t accept “just tired”; creates space for her own account.
Traumatic forceps delivery, no family nearby, breastfeeding, partner relationship, idealised expectations of motherhood.
Two depression identification questions; EPDS or PHQ-9 as a supporting measure; mental state including psychotic features.
Baby blues versus postnatal depression versus postpartum psychosis; considers birth-related trauma and anxiety.
Explicit questions on suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, thoughts of harm to the baby, care of the baby, and psychotic symptoms.
Names postnatal depression with intrusive thoughts, clearly separated from intent to harm.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Perinatal psychological therapy (NICE CG192); antidepressant option compatible with breastfeeding discussed; her choice respected.
Birth trauma acknowledged; health visitor and partner involved with consent; isolation addressed.
Crisis routes (practice, NHS 111 mental health option, 999); review within a week; risk discussion documented.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Partner’s concern, flat affect, “terrible mother” and the hesitation about thoughts are all followed up.
Idea (normal tiredness); concern (the baby will be taken away); expectation (to be told she’s fine).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror that admitting she’s struggling means social services will take the baby and she’ll be judged an unfit mother; this is why she hides the intrusive thoughts and minimises; trauma from the delivery, isolation, and shame about not bonding — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Aisha, I’m Dr Shah. Can you hear me alright, and are you somewhere private? … Thanks for booking. How have things been since the baby arrived?
model.why: Checks privacy on video and opens broadly

model.text: Honestly, I don’t know why he made such a fuss. I’m fine, just tired. All new mums are, aren’t they? Can you just tell him I’m okay so he stops hovering?
Being exhausted with a new baby is really common. Your partner sees you every day, and I’d like to hear from you how things really are, with no rush. Is that okay?
model.why: Normalises tiredness while treating the partner’s concern as meaningful, without colluding

model.text: I suppose.
Over the last few weeks, how has your mood been most days? And are you still able to enjoy things, even small things?
model.why: Asks the two core depression questions naturally (NICE CG192)

model.text: …Not really. I cry a lot. I don’t enjoy anything. Even when he sleeps, I can’t.
That sounds really hard. How long has it been like this? And how are you eating, and concentrating?
model.why: Establishes duration beyond the blues and biological symptoms

model.text: About a month, maybe longer. I’m not hungry. I can’t think straight. I feel like a terrible mother.
What makes you feel that?
model.why: Follows the guilt cue rather than reassuring it away

model.text: I don’t feel what I’m supposed to feel. Everyone says you fall in love with them straight away. I just feel… far away from him.
Thank you for telling me. Feeling detached is a common part of postnatal depression, and it isn’t a sign you’re a bad mother. How was the birth for you?
model.why: Normalises detachment and opens the birth experience

model.text: Awful. It ended with forceps. I haven’t really talked about it. We haven’t got family nearby.
I ask every mum who feels this low some important questions. When things are at their worst, do you ever feel your family would be better off without you, or have thoughts of harming yourself?
model.why: Asks directly about suicidal thoughts, framed as routine

model.text: …Sometimes I think they’d be better off without me. I wouldn’t do anything. I just think it.
Thank you for being honest. Have you made any plans, or thought about how? And what keeps you going?
model.why: Explores plan, intent and protective factors without assuming them

model.text: No. No plans. It’s just a feeling that comes.
Sometimes mums get frightening thoughts that pop into their head, like something bad happening to the baby, and the thoughts horrify them. Has anything like that happened to you?
model.why: Asks about intrusive thoughts of harm to the baby in a normalising way

model.text: (tearful) Yes. Awful pictures. I’d never hurt him. I haven’t told anyone because… they’d take him away.

I’m really glad you told me. Thoughts like that, which frighten you, are a known symptom of postnatal depression and anxiety. They don’t mean you would act on them. Have you had any times where things seemed unreal, or you heard or saw things others didn’t?
model.why: Separates intrusive thoughts from intent and screens for psychosis

model.text: No. Nothing like that.

Can I come back to what you said about the baby being taken away? That’s a very common fear, and I want to be clear: getting help is what good mums do. Our job is to help you get well while you look after him. Nothing you’ve told me today makes me think he’s unsafe with you.
model.why: Dismantles the hidden fear honestly and directly

model.text: Really? I thought if I said anything…

Really. What you’re describing — a month of low mood, no enjoyment, poor sleep and appetite, the guilt and the frightening thoughts — is postnatal depression. It’s an illness, it’s common, and it gets better with treatment.
model.why: Names the diagnosis clearly with the reasoning

model.text: There are a few options. Talking therapy for new mums is very effective, and I’d like to refer you to the perinatal mental health team. Some women also take an antidepressant; there are ones we commonly use while breastfeeding. What feels right to you?
model.why: Shares options including breastfeeding-compatible medication and invites her preference

model.text: I’d like the talking. I’m not sure about tablets yet.
That’s a good start and we can revisit tablets at any time. I’d also like your health visitor to know so she can support you, and would you be happy for your partner to be part of the plan?
model.why: Builds a support network with her consent

model.text: Yes. I think I need to tell him properly.

If the thoughts of not being here get stronger, or you feel you might act on any thought about yourself or the baby, ring us straight away, NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999. I’ll send you the numbers. I’d like to speak again within a week.
model.why: Specific crisis routes and early review

model.text: Before we finish, what will you tell your partner about today?
model.why: Teach-back framed around the conversation she needs to have

model.text: That it’s postnatal depression, it’s treatable, I’m getting talking therapy, and I’m not a bad mum.
That’s exactly it. You came in wanting me to say you were fine. What I’m saying is you’re not alone, and you’ll feel like yourself again.
model.why: Closes by addressing her original request with hope

social.t: No family nearby and an unprocessed forceps delivery add to her risk. Ask what practical help exists and who she can talk to.
Her partner noticed first. With her consent, involve him in the plan and the safety-net.

legal.t: The child’s welfare is paramount, but maternal depression alone is not a safeguarding concern. Refer if there is a risk to the baby (for example intent to harm or inability to care). Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023).
She is an adult with capacity. Share information with her partner only with her agreement, unless there is a serious risk to her or the baby. GMC Confidentiality (2017).

professional.t: Asking about suicide does not increase risk. Record the questions, her answers, protective factors and the safety plan (NICE NG225).
Tell the health visitor (with consent) and use the specialist perinatal mental health pathway. Honest explanation of how services work reduces concealment.

community.t: PANDAS Foundation, Mind, the Association for Post Natal Illness; local NHS Talking Therapies with perinatal priority; Samaritans 116 123.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, with plan, intent or means
Thoughts of harming the baby with intent, or inability to care for the baby
Sudden confusion, perplexity, mania, delusions or hallucinations: possible postpartum psychosis, assessment within 4 hours (NICE CG192)
psychosocial: Traumatic forceps birth she has not talked about
No family nearby; relies on her partner
Shame about not feeling the expected bond; breastfeeding
ice: Idea: “I’m just tired like every new mum”
Concern: if she admits it, the baby will be taken away
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her partner stops worrying

playbook.diagnosis: “A month of low mood, not enjoying anything, poor sleep and appetite, guilt and frightening thoughts is postnatal depression. It’s common, it’s an illness, and it responds to treatment.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Postnatal depression is like a heavy fog that settles after the birth. It changes how you feel about yourself and even the baby, but it isn’t who you are, and it lifts with the right help.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried that telling me would mean losing your baby. It doesn’t. Asking for help is what a caring mum does, and our aim is to get you well at home with him.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the birth and the isolation; involve her partner and the health visitor with consent; let her choose between therapy alone and therapy with medication.
sharedPlan: Referral to the perinatal mental health team and psychological therapy (NICE CG192)
Antidepressant option discussed with breastfeeding in mind; check the BNF; her choice to start with therapy
Health visitor informed; partner involved; review within a week
safetyNet: Practice, NHS 111 mental health option or 999 if thoughts of self-harm grow or she fears acting on any thought
Same-day contact for confusion, not sleeping at all, or seeing or hearing things

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by colluding with “just tired”, by avoiding the risk questions, or by reacting to the intrusive thoughts in a way that confirms her fear. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Agrees it’s normal tiredness and advises rest.
items.why: “Did not reach an appropriate working diagnosis.” The duration and features go well beyond the blues.
items.fix: Ask the two core questions and about sleep when the baby sleeps, guilt and bonding.

items.fail: Never asks about suicidal thoughts or thoughts about the baby.
items.why: “Did not assess risk.” This is the non-negotiable task in any perinatal mood station.
items.fix: Ask every risk question directly, framed as routine: self, baby, psychosis, and care of the baby.

items.fail: Reacts with visible alarm to the intrusive thoughts and mentions social services.
items.why: Confirms her hidden fear and shuts down disclosure. Horrifying intrusive thoughts are a symptom, not intent.
items.fix: Thank her, explain what intrusive thoughts are, check intent calmly, and say plainly that help is about keeping them together.

items.fail: Tells her “you’re not a terrible mother” and moves on.
items.why: Reassurance without exploration misses the detachment and birth trauma behind the guilt.
items.fix: “What makes you feel that?” Then name detachment as part of the illness.

items.fail: States that antidepressants can’t be used while breastfeeding, or prescribes without mentioning it.
items.why: Either error is unsafe or removes a valid option.
items.fix: Offer psychological therapy and discuss an antidepressant, checking the BNF breastfeeding advice, as her choice.

items.fail: Closes with “come back if you feel worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting after disclosed suicidal thoughts is a clear failing point.
items.fix: Named crisis routes, the psychosis warning signs, review within a week, and teach-back.

timeMap.d: Check privacy. She opens by minimising. Don’t agree and don’t argue; ask for her own account.
Mood, enjoyment, sleep when the baby sleeps, appetite, concentration, guilt, bonding, the birth, support.
Suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, protective factors. Intrusive thoughts about the baby. Psychotic features. Care of the baby.
Name and dismantle the fear of the baby being taken. Then name postnatal depression.
Perinatal therapy, medication option with breastfeeding, health visitor and partner. Crisis numbers. Review within a week. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Reassures that exhaustion is normal and suggests more sleep; never asks about suicidal thoughts or thoughts about the baby; misses the fear of removal; or, having heard about intrusive thoughts, reacts with alarm and mentions social services first.
wordPics.pass: Recognises postnatal depression, asks directly about self-harm and harm to the baby, screens for psychosis, offers perinatal therapy and follow-up with a crisis safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus the intrusive thoughts are received calmly and explained, the fear of removal is named and dismantled, the birth trauma is acknowledged, medication is discussed with breastfeeding in mind, she chooses the plan, and the partner becomes part of the support.

avoid.dont: “Every new mum feels like this. Try to rest when the baby sleeps.”
avoid.instead: “Tiredness is normal, but not enjoying anything and feeling a terrible mother for a month is more than that. Tell me more.”
avoid.why: Normalising closes the door she is hoping you’ll open.

avoid.dont: “Thoughts about harming the baby? I’ll need to involve social services.”
avoid.instead: “Frightening thoughts like that are a known symptom. They don’t mean you would act on them, and I’m glad you told me.”
avoid.why: Horrifying intrusive thoughts are not intent. Leading with safeguarding confirms her worst fear and ends disclosure.

avoid.instead: “Some antidepressants are commonly used while breastfeeding; we can look at that together if you want it.”
avoid.why: Wrong information removes a legitimate option.

SCA_MODELS.why: Dismantles the hidden fear honestly and directly

SCA_MODELS.text: Really? I thought if I said anything…

Really. What you’re describing — a month of low mood, no enjoyment, poor sleep and appetite, the guilt and the frightening thoughts — is postnatal depression. It’s an illness, it’s common, and it gets better with treatment.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the diagnosis clearly with the reasoning

SCA_MODELS.text: There are a few options. Talking therapy for new mums is very effective, and I’d like to refer you to the perinatal mental health team. Some women also take an antidepressant; there are ones we commonly use while breastfeeding. What feels right to you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares options including breastfeeding-compatible medication and invites her preference

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d like the talking. I’m not sure about tablets yet.
That’s a good start and we can revisit tablets at any time. I’d also like your health visitor to know so she can support you, and would you be happy for your partner to be part of the plan?
SCA_MODELS.why: Builds a support network with her consent

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I think I need to tell him properly.

If the thoughts of not being here get stronger, or you feel you might act on any thought about yourself or the baby, ring us straight away, NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999. I’ll send you the numbers. I’d like to speak again within a week.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific crisis routes and early review

SCA_MODELS.text: Before we finish, what will you tell your partner about today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back framed around the conversation she needs to have

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s postnatal depression, it’s treatable, I’m getting talking therapy, and I’m not a bad mum.
That’s exactly it. You came in wanting me to say you were fine. What I’m saying is you’re not alone, and you’ll feel like yourself again.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes by addressing her original request with hope

SCA_STEM.name: Aisha Rahman
pmh: First baby 8 weeks ago: forceps delivery
SCA_STEM.recent: Delivered 8 weeks ago (forceps). Breastfeeding. Appointment booked at her partner’s request.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation. Partner concerned she is “not herself”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health · NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Low mood, loss of interest, guilt and detachment from the baby 8 weeks after birth is postnatal depression, not tiredness. Ask directly about thoughts of self-harm and of harm to the baby, screen for psychosis, and deal with the fear of the baby being taken away.

points.t: Baby blues are common in the first days after birth and settle within about 2 weeks. Symptoms lasting longer, with anhedonia, guilt, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and poor bonding, indicate a depressive episode.

NICE CG192: at contact in the postnatal period, ask the two depression identification questions (feeling down, depressed or hopeless; little interest or pleasure) and consider the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment. Tools support clinical judgement; they do not replace it.

Ask about thoughts of self-harm or suicide (plan, intent, means), thoughts of harm to the baby, intrusive thoughts, and her ability to care for the baby. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or low, medium or high ratings to predict suicide; build a safety plan around her needs.

Sudden onset of confusion, perplexity, mania, delusions or hallucinations is an emergency. NICE CG192: refer to secondary mental health services, preferably the specialist perinatal team, for assessment within 4 hours.

NICE CG192: for moderate or severe depression in the postnatal period, offer a high-intensity psychological intervention such as CBT; consider an antidepressant if she prefers medication, declines therapy or symptoms have not responded. Discuss breastfeeding: check the BNF breastfeeding advice for the chosen drug (sertraline is often chosen). Dose per BNF.

Fear that social services will take the baby is a common reason mothers hide symptoms. Most mothers with postnatal depression receive support to recover while caring for their baby; a safeguarding referral is made only where there is a risk to the child.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about life since the birth; doesn’t accept “just tired”; creates space for her own account.
Traumatic forceps delivery, no family nearby, breastfeeding, partner relationship, idealised expectations of motherhood.
Partner’s concern, flat affect, “terrible mother” and the hesitation about thoughts are all followed up.
Idea (normal tiredness); concern (the baby will be taken away); expectation (to be told she’s fine).
Two depression identification questions; EPDS or PHQ-9 as a supporting measure; mental state including psychotic features.
Baby blues versus postnatal depression versus postpartum psychosis; considers birth-related trauma and anxiety.
Explicit questions on suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, thoughts of harm to the baby, care of the baby, and psychotic symptoms.
Names postnatal depression with intrusive thoughts, clearly separated from intent to harm.
Perinatal psychological therapy (NICE CG192); antidepressant option compatible with breastfeeding discussed; her choice respected.
Birth trauma acknowledged; health visitor and partner involved with consent; isolation addressed.
Crisis routes (practice, NHS 111 mental health option, 999); review within a week; risk discussion documented.

social.t: No family nearby and an unprocessed forceps delivery add to her risk. Ask what practical help exists and who she can talk to.
Her partner noticed first. With her consent, involve him in the plan and the safety-net.

legal.t: The child’s welfare is paramount, but maternal depression alone is not a safeguarding concern. Refer if there is a risk to the baby (for example intent to harm or inability to care). Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023).
She is an adult with capacity. Share information with her partner only with her agreement, unless there is a serious risk to her or the baby. GMC Confidentiality (2017).

professional.t: Asking about suicide does not increase risk. Record the questions, her answers, protective factors and the safety plan (NICE NG225).
Tell the health visitor (with consent) and use the specialist perinatal mental health pathway. Honest explanation of how services work reduces concealment.

community.t: PANDAS Foundation, Mind, the Association for Post Natal Illness; local NHS Talking Therapies with perinatal priority; Samaritans 116 123.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, with plan, intent or means
Thoughts of harming the baby with intent, or inability to care for the baby
Sudden confusion, perplexity, mania, delusions or hallucinations: possible postpartum psychosis, assessment within 4 hours (NICE CG192)
psychosocial: Traumatic forceps birth she has not talked about
No family nearby; relies on her partner
Shame about not feeling the expected bond; breastfeeding
ice: Idea: “I’m just tired like every new mum”
Concern: if she admits it, the baby will be taken away
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her partner stops worrying

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “A month of low mood, not enjoying anything, poor sleep and appetite, guilt and frightening thoughts is postnatal depression. It’s common, it’s an illness, and it responds to treatment.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Postnatal depression is like a heavy fog that settles after the birth. It changes how you feel about yourself and even the baby, but it isn’t who you are, and it lifts with the right help.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried that telling me would mean losing your baby. It doesn’t. Asking for help is what a caring mum does, and our aim is to get you well at home with him.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the birth and the isolation; involve her partner and the health visitor with consent; let her choose between therapy alone and therapy with medication.
sharedPlan: Referral to the perinatal mental health team and psychological therapy (NICE CG192)
Antidepressant option discussed with breastfeeding in mind; check the BNF; her choice to start with therapy
Health visitor informed; partner involved; review within a week
safetyNet: Practice, NHS 111 mental health option or 999 if thoughts of self-harm grow or she fears acting on any thought
Same-day contact for confusion, not sleeping at all, or seeing or hearing things

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by colluding with “just tired”, by avoiding the risk questions, or by reacting to the intrusive thoughts in a way that confirms her fear. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Agrees it’s normal tiredness and advises rest.
items.why: “Did not reach an appropriate working diagnosis.” The duration and features go well beyond the blues.
items.fix: Ask the two core questions and about sleep when the baby sleeps, guilt and bonding.

items.fail: Never asks about suicidal thoughts or thoughts about the baby.
items.why: “Did not assess risk.” This is the non-negotiable task in any perinatal mood station.
items.fix: Ask every risk question directly, framed as routine: self, baby, psychosis, and care of the baby.

items.fail: Reacts with visible alarm to the intrusive thoughts and mentions social services.
items.why: Confirms her hidden fear and shuts down disclosure. Horrifying intrusive thoughts are a symptom, not intent.
items.fix: Thank her, explain what intrusive thoughts are, check intent calmly, and say plainly that help is about keeping them together.

items.fail: Tells her “you’re not a terrible mother” and moves on.
items.why: Reassurance without exploration misses the detachment and birth trauma behind the guilt.
items.fix: “What makes you feel that?” Then name detachment as part of the illness.

items.fail: States that antidepressants can’t be used while breastfeeding, or prescribes without mentioning it.
items.why: Either error is unsafe or removes a valid option.
items.fix: Offer psychological therapy and discuss an antidepressant, checking the BNF breastfeeding advice, as her choice.

items.fail: Closes with “come back if you feel worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting after disclosed suicidal thoughts is a clear failing point.
items.fix: Named crisis routes, the psychosis warning signs, review within a week, and teach-back.
